content: Neonates are at an increased risk of infection due to their immature immune systems. The transfer of maternal immunoglobulins to the fetus primarily occurs after 32 weeks of gestation, and the neonate’s own production of immunoglobulins begins several months after birth. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) administration provides immunoglobulin G (IgG), which can bind to cell surface receptors, enhance opsonization, activate the complement system, promote antibody-dependent cytotoxicity, and improve neutrophil chemiluminescence. Theoretically, these mechanisms could reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with infections in neonates. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of IVIG on mortality and morbidity in neonates with suspected or confirmed infections at the time of study entry. Additionally, a subgroup analysis was conducted to assess the impact of IgM-enriched IVIG on mortality in cases of suspected infection. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, The Cochrane Library, CINAHL, trial registries, and Web of Science, as well as through reference lists of identified studies and personal files. The search was updated in 2013, and no language restrictions were applied. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving neonates less than 28 days old. The trials compared IVIG treatment for suspected or confirmed bacterial or fungal infections with either placebo or no intervention. Outcomes assessed included mortality, length of hospital stay, and psychomotor development at follow-up. Statistical analyses included calculations of typical risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), weighted mean differences (WMD), and the number needed to treat for an additional beneficial or harmful outcome (NNTB or NNTH), all with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The I² statistic was used to assess statistical heterogeneity. The updated search identified one additional study that had been ongoing. In total, nine studies involving 3,973 neonates were included in the review. The results showed that IVIG treatment did not significantly reduce mortality during the hospital stay in neonates with clinically suspected infections (9 studies, n = 2,527; RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.13; RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.02; I² = 23% for RR and 29% for RD). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the combined outcome of death or major disability at two years of corrected age in neonates with suspected infections (1 study, n = 1,985; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.09; RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.03). For neonates with confirmed infections at the time of trial entry, IVIG treatment did not significantly reduce mortality during the hospital stay (1 trial, n = 1,446; RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.21; RD -0.01, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.03) or the combined outcome of death or major disability at two years of corrected age (1 trial, n = 1,393; RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.18; RD 0.01, 95% CI -0.04 to 0.06). When considering neonates with either suspected or confirmed infections at trial entry, IVIG treatment did not significantly affect mortality during the hospital stay (1 study, n = 3,493; RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.16; RD 0.00, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.03) or the combined outcome of death or major disability at two years of corrected age (1 study, n = 3,493; RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.09; RD 0.00, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.03). Additionally, IVIG treatment did not reduce the length of hospital stay in neonates with suspected or confirmed infections (1 study, n = 3,493; mean difference 0.00 days, 95% CI -0.61 to 0.61). The administration of IgM-enriched IVIG for suspected infections also did not significantly reduce mortality during the hospital stay (4 studies, n = 266; RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.20; RD -0.06, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.02; I² = 17% for RR and 53% for RD). The authors concluded that the results of the INIS trial, which included 3,493 neonates, along with the meta-analysis of 3,973 neonates, demonstrated no reduction in mortality during the hospital stay or in the combined outcome of death or major disability at two years of corrected age in neonates with suspected or confirmed infections. Furthermore, the evidence from a smaller sample size (n = 266) indicated that IgM-enriched IVIG does not significantly reduce mortality during the hospital stay in neonates with suspected infections. Based on these findings, routine administration of IVIG or IgM-enriched IVIG to prevent mortality in neonates with suspected or confirmed infections is not recommended. No further research in this area is suggested.
